extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsrooms, editors, journalism educators and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial guidelines and standards for practising constructive journalism in newsrooms — an approach that goes beyond negativity bias by emphasising solutions, nuance, and democratic conversation. Covers story selection, interview style, tone, and what constructive journalism is and is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Three Pillars
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism is built on three foundational pillars: solutions, nuance and democratic conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These pillars are presented as the foundation of constructive journalism practice and should guide selection, reporting, tone, and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism highlights responses to well-documented problems, changing the focus of the story from the problem itself to the efforts to solve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is rigorous and critical in its coverage of both problems and progress. It aims to 'rigorously report on potential solutions' and is not activism, feel‑good human interest, or rose‑tinted reporting. (See examples: 'How To Incorporate Solution-Focused Stories into Radio Newscasts' — NDR, Germany.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting should be balanced, fair, non-sensational and calm in tone, embracing complexity rather than portraying issues in black and white.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to help the public develop an accurate understanding of the world by providing complete, nuanced narratives instead of simplified ones. (See example: 'How To Embrace Nuance in Political Coverage' — Berlingske, Denmark.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote democratic conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism seeks to strengthen democracy and counter political polarization by promoting civil discourse, engaging audiences, and building trust in the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should enable critical but constructive debate about potential solutions without taking sides or igniting conflict. (Example: ZEIT ONLINE's 'My Country Talks' project; 'How To Host A Civil And Curious Political Debate Show' — NRK, Norway.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'if it bleeds, it leads' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism intentionally goes beyond the sensationalism and negativity bias that prioritizes conflict, scandal, and outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should avoid defaulting to clickbait, outrage-driven content, and disproportionate negativity; instead add context and perspective to reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection: include 'What Now?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Story selection should go beyond the traditional 5 W's (Who, What, When, Where, Why) to include 'What Now?' — i.e., what responses, developments or solutions exist or are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reframing steers coverage toward future-oriented, constructive angles and informs newsroom editorial decisions and prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews: shift from accusatory to curious and open-minded
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews should be conducted with curiosity and openness rather than accusatory or adversarial framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change aims to surface explanations, responses, and possibilities rather than only confrontation; it affects sourcing, questioning style, and relationships with interviewees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic style: move from dramatic/critical to curious
rubrics_metrics.description: The stylistic tone of coverage should favour curiosity and exploration over dramatic, sensational, or cynically critical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt calmer tone, avoid tabloid-style scandals and outrage-driven phrasing; allow complexity and context to shape narrative voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role redefinition: facilitators of conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should change their relationship with audiences from mere disseminators of information to facilitators of conversations with experts and those in power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies more engagement, two-way formats, and active efforts to foster public deliberation and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political coverage: focus less on horse-race metrics and more on voter-relevant detail
rubrics_metrics.description: In political reporting, de-emphasise horse-race election coverage (poll standings, fundraising) and instead focus on the details voters need to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This steers politicians toward concrete proposals and away from partisan talking points; helps citizens evaluate policy implications rather than personality or short-term metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aiming to be critical, objective and balanced
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism explicitly aims to remain critical, objective and balanced in its reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being constructive does not mean abandoning critique; rigorous standards and critical assessment remain central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing important societal issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism prioritizes reporting on important societal issues rather than trivial or purely entertaining topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus editorial resources on matters that affect communities, governance, and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Based on facts and unbiased
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism must be based on facts and maintain lack of bias in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorously verify evidence, avoid partisan slant, and ensure factual foundations for solution-focused or future-oriented reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage should be calm in tone, resisting sensationalistic affect and outrage-driven language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A calm tone helps audiences receive complex information without heightening polarization or despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resists sensationalism and outrage
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism actively resists sensationalism, outrage, and the incentives that amplify negative extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial processes should counteract algorithms and formats that reward outrage, focusing instead on informative and contextual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging, not polarizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach seeks to bridge divides rather than deepen political or social polarization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reporting formats and framing that encourage understanding across differences (e.g., facilitated dialogues, balanced representation of views).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking and future-oriented
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism adopts a forward-looking stance, aiming to leave audiences inspired, hopeful, and motivated toward solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While documenting problems, coverage should also explore trajectories, responses, and what could come next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced and contextualized
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should be nuanced and contextualized — placing issues in broader perspective and relevant context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide background, data, and multiple perspectives so audiences can evaluate complexity rather than relying on simplified narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not promoting a specific agenda or blurring journalism and politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism must not promote a specific political agenda or mix advocacy with reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear boundary between reporting and activism; avoid editorializing solutions as partisan prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not uncritical or naive
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism is not uncritical or naive about actors, proposals, or outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain skepticism, verification and critical evaluation even when covering positive responses or solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not glorifying individuals, governments or civil society organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not engage in uncritical praise or hero-worship of people or institutions involved in solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance coverage of actors' contributions with scrutiny of limitations, trade-offs, and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not suppressing critical perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism must not suppress dissenting or critical viewpoints for the sake of positivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include critical voices and evaluation of solutions; constructiveness requires honesty about shortcomings and risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not engaging in activism of any kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly avoid journalistic activism; constructive reporting should inform democratic decision-making without campaigning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep reporting distinct from advocacy and campaigning; provide information that enables public deliberation rather than promoting a cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not dumbed-down, trivial or 'happy news'
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism is not about trivial 'happy' news or diluting seriousness for feel-good stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid superficial positivity; focus on substantial, evidence-based reporting about responses and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not giving in to false equivalence/balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not create false balance between viewpoints when evidence does not warrant equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize and weight perspectives according to evidence rather than offering symmetry for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not advocating one solution over others
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive coverage should not uncritically endorse a single solution as the only option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on multiple responses, trade-offs, evidence base, and uncertainties so audiences can weigh alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not oversimplifying complex problems or solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid simplifying complex social problems or their potential solutions into reductive narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context, caveats, and complexity — recognise uncertainty and constraints in reporting on solutions.
